label: Precursors + ACID breakthrough
summary: Evidence supports a precursor phase around Myo Kyawt Myaing and late-1990s Yangon nightclub culture. ACID's 2000 Sa Tin Chin / Beginning is the widely reported breakthrough, but 'first' remains an attributed claim, not an exhaustive proof.
eventNotes: Late-1990s ACID nightclub origins
2000 - Sa Tin Chin / Beginning
facts: Htein Lin's historical account calls Myo Kyawt Myaing generally considered Burmese rap's godfather, while Apple Music displays a 1994 rap-labelled catalogue date that still needs original-release verification.
Multiple reputable retrospective sources date ACID's Sa Tin Chin / SaTin Gyin / Sa-Tin-Chein (Beginning) to 2000 and describe it as an immediate, chart-leading landmark.
ACID's four-member founding line-up is reported as Anegga/Annaga, Hein Zaw, Yan Yan Chan, and Phyo Zeya Thaw/Zayar Thaw.

label: Underground consolidation
summary: A youth-facing underground ecology grew under censorship. 'Second generation' is retained as a retrospective community label, not a fixed canon. Snare/Nay Win offers the clearest date-specific DIY release trail.
eventNotes: 2001 - Snare's 40-copy home album
2005 - Hip Hop Vibration VCD account
facts: Nay Win says Snare formed in 2000 and recorded a 40-copy unofficial home album in 2001 with a computer microphone.
Nay Win says arrests around 2003-04 disrupted Snare's next project, and describes a 2005 Hip Hop Vibration VCD release; the solo/group credit remains unresolved.
The recurring 9mm / Project-1 / Firecracker / Examplz / On-Track / Cyclone / M.H.A. roster comes mostly from community or tertiary histories and still needs act-by-act primary verification.
confidence: high for Snare / low for roster

label: 3G claims + mixed circulation
summary: Late-2000s rap circulated through home-recorded demos, bootlegs, live shows and web video while official channels remained censored. 'Third generation' is a self-applied/secondary label, not a settled canon, and the same period is where the underground tape ecosystem becomes visible in the archive: B-Clipz, M.R.C and the Y.H.S studio in Yangon, Wildboy in Mandalay, and a proliferation of mixtapes and VCDs that no streaming platform has ever catalogued.
eventNotes: 2007 - Generation Wave forms after the Saffron Revolution crackdown
2009-2013 - Wildboy active in Mandalay; Wildboyz mixtape Feb 2013
2010 - Never Give Up video / activist music
2011-2014 - B-Clipz, M.R.C and Y.H.S release mixtapes and songs in Yangon
facts: A 2010 scholarly account documents near-weekly cool-season shows, stage-show bootlegs, home demos, and uploads to Burmesemtv.com - a mixed ecology, not a streaming-first scene.
The specific late-2006 third-generation self-identification and VIP/Rock$tar roster are weakly sourced; the archive keeps those names visibly qualified.
Generation Wave was an adjacent pro-democracy youth network using music, graffiti and pamphlets. It should not be collapsed into every third-wave rap act.

B-Clipz, formed in Yangon in August 2008 with nine members, never released an album: Aung Ye' Htike reports the group circulated songs plus planned mixtapes, and that he produced around 20 songs in 2011 alone. Mandalay's Wildboy released a 12-track mixtape in February 2013.

The archived fan channels that catalogued this era - Myanmar Hip Hop Channel, the Myanmar Hip Hop Underground blog and myanmarmp3album.com - are the only source for most of these releases. Several of those domains are now dead or hijacked and are cited through web.archive.org only.
confidence: high for circulation / low for canon

label: Reform era, underground tape scene and the fourth generation
kicker: TAPES, PARKS, AND THE LABEL YEARS
summary: The 2012 end of pre-publication censorship widened room for music, but legal restrictions, self-censorship, permits and weak venues remained. This is also the decade the underground tape scene is best documented: Mandalay's Wildboy produced Oasix and Y-Zet, while Yangon ran on mixtapes, VCDs and small live platforms such as Jam It! and the Full Stop shows. By 2017 a fourth generation had arrived in the form of Yung Hugo, X-Boxin, Htet Yan, Zay Ye' and the BG18 circle, and the live scene had contracted from big-hotel bills to park shows and hotel residencies.
eventNotes: 2012 - pre-publication media censorship ends
2012 - Jam It! first show, Kan Daw Gyi Park
2015 - 'Pyaw San Par' duo album; nationwide recognition
2016 - FIRST STEP at Myaw Sin Island; Monsoon II at the Yangon International Hotel; Straight Outta Yangon Round 3
2017 - Straight Outta Yangon Chapter 2, ACID reunion; Y-Zet promotion in Mandalay turns violent
2018 - X-Boxin album 99; Oasix album 1992; Htet Yan and Thar Thar's 'Nway Thwar Tal'
2019 - Break the Night, French Institute Yangon; Adjustor's Compoptable
facts: BBC and Human Rights Watch date the end of pre-publication media censorship to 20 August 2012, while also documenting continued restrictive laws and self-censorship.

Oasix and Y-Zet both came out of Mandalay's Wildboy crew, then released the duet album 'Pyaw San Par' on 24 December 2015, which gave Oasix nationwide recognition. Oasix's own biography titles his 2009-2013 phase 'Career beginnings in underground'.

Jam It!, founded by Eaiddhi and Ye Ngwe Soe, started as an acoustic gig in Kan Daw Gyi Park in late 2012 and had run 20+ gigs across Yangon and Mandalay by 2015 with 40+ acts, cross-genre with punk, metal and live graffiti. It is the best-documented underground live platform in the archive.

Yung Hugo's Make Karen Great Again (2023) is a Karen-language album, marking ethnic-language rap as distinct from the Yangon-centre framing of earlier periods. He describes 2010-2015 as 'the golden age of hip hop' but says he was told there were no shows, and wants to rebuild it.

The live scene contracted rather than disappeared: free park shows at Myaw Sin Island in 2016 sat alongside paid hotel residencies, and the 2017 Y-Zet album promotion in Mandalay turned violent, killing a 19-year-old.

The Global Voices-era reporting on Y.A.K., Ko Minn and Jam It! documents a scene more regional and self-organised than a single Yangon mainstream. Several acts named in this period came from the pop or mainstream sphere rather than the underground tape circuit; the archive keeps that distinction visible in artistNames rather than promoting them.

The earliest record here is physical: Jimmy Jacobs handed out CDs and cassettes at his shows when internet access in Myanmar was still limited, which is the clearest single document of the distribution era the fourth generation came out of.
confidence: high for the tape-era and Wildboy story / medium for the 4G framing

label: Post-coup resistance + current scene
summary: After the 1 February 2021 coup, rap became the most visible form of cultural resistance, and the scene split along three lines at once. Rap Against Junta grew from street concerts in Yangon and released DICKCOUNCIL in October 2021 while the country had no reliable internet. The BG18 label circle in Yangon carried on releasing - Adjustor, GRACEe, Yung Hugo - and Yung Hugo's 2023 Make Karen Great Again was a Karen-language album. A diaspora strand moved to Chiang Mai, where Kan Kyi organises MOB Party, and to Indianapolis, where Vanzzzo released 'Rebel (Save Myanmar)'. Separately, a new wave organised by label rather than crew took hold in Yangon, from Lil Kee Boi's Bago-to-Munich trap through 223, Ah Sar, Myat Amara Maung and Reload. No canonical 2021-2026 generation is asserted, and the sources do not agree on one.
eventNotes: 2021-02 - first RAJ street show, Yangon
2021-10-21 - DICKCOUNCIL listening party, streamed on YouTube
2022-07-25 - Phyo Zeya Thaw executed; 'Generation Driven by Faith' released posthumously 2023
2023-08-24 - Byu Har sentenced to 20 years
2024-11-30 and 2025-11-29 - MOB Party, Chiang Mai
2025-11-02 - Overflow Music Festival, Yangon; 16 charged
facts: The 1 February 2021 coup was followed within weeks by dozens of anti-military tracks across Facebook, YouTube and SoundCloud; Facebook itself was blocked 4-7 February 2021 and the country then lost the internet for weeks, with 46 consecutive nights of wireless blackout before a full national cut from 1 April.

Rap Against Junta is best represented as a decentralised alliance of MCs, producers, DJs, sound engineers, dancers, promoters, organisers and graffiti artists, insisting 'We are all leaders'. VICE names Osho - an alias adopted to protect his identity - as the originator. Its DICKCOUNCIL track count is genuinely disputed: Bandcamp and HipHopDX say 12, RAJ's own statement says 11 songs by 15 rappers, and the archive preserves both.

Byu Har, described by the BBC as one of Myanmar's biggest hip-hop artists, was arrested in May 2023 after a Facebook Live criticising power cuts and sentenced to 20 years in August. He is not a member of Rap Against Junta.

DVB documents MOB Party in Chiang Mai in 2024 and 2025 with Thai, Myanmar and international participation. Of nine countries checked for a Burmese rap scene, only Thailand has a documented one and it is documented by a single outlet; seven have nothing at all, which is a finding rather than an oversight.

The 2020s new wave is organised by label rather than crew or city: Billionaire Minds Group dominates, with Eagle Element and b4 Records alongside it. Drill and Jersey Club are the new sounds, per LIFTED's 2023 scene report.

Phyo Zeya Thaw, ACID co-founder and Generation Wave member, was executed on 25 July 2022. Rap Against Junta later released his unfinished 'Generation Driven by Faith', built around a prison voice note in which he says he never completed it.
